guide.title: Durham, Connecticut: A Farming Town's Second-Oldest Library
guide.intro: Durham was settled in 1699, formally named in May 1708 and incorporated as a town that October. The area was originally called Coginchaug, a Native American word meaning "long swamp," frequented by the Mattabesett people; the English name comes from Durham, England. From its earliest days Durham was largely a farming community, and it remains agricultural in character today. In 1733 — one year after Benjamin Franklin organized his Philadelphia book club — Durham residents founded the Durham Book Company, which the town's library describes as the second-oldest lending library in the country and the oldest in New England; it dissolved in the 1830s, but 39 of its original volumes survive in the local history collection. Moses Austin, father of Stephen F. Austin, the "Father of Texas," was born in Durham in 1761. The Durham Fair, founded in 1916, has grown into Connecticut's largest agricultural fair.

sections.heading: A farming town's library and fair
sections.body: Durham's 1733 Durham Book Company dissolved in the 1830s as newspapers and magazines proliferated, but 39 of its volumes were later recovered for the local history collection. The modern Durham Public Library traces to an 1894 town vote; Mrs. Charles G. Rockwood donated land on condition that a building costing at least $3,000 be erected, and the library that resulted opened in 1902, served the town for 83 years before its first addition, and expanded again in 1997. Durham has two National Register listings: the Thomas Lyman House on Middlefield Road (1975) and the Main Street Historic District (1986), whose colonial-era village core the town's America 250 Committee tours periodically on foot. The Durham Fair, founded in 1916 and run 100% by volunteers, has grown into Connecticut's largest agricultural fair — interrupted only by 1938 hurricane damage, World War II and the 2020 pandemic.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Durham has no interstate and no rail station of its own. Connecticut Route 17 is the two-lane spine running from I-91 in New Haven north through Durham to Middletown and on to Route 2 in Glastonbury, with Route 68 crossing east–west and Routes 77, 79 and 147 running south to Guilford, south to Madison, and north into Middlefield. The nearest passenger rail is the CTrail Hartford Line at Meriden or Wallingford, or Shore Line East at Guilford or Madison.

sections.heading: The Durham Fair and outdoor Durham
sections.body: The 2026 Durham Fair, the 106th annual, runs September 24–27 with livestock and agricultural competitions, tractor pulls, rides and live music; admission is $10 Thursday, $20 Friday–Sunday ($10 for seniors 65+), with children 11 and under, active military and wheelchair users admitted free. Millers Pond State Park offers an easy, flat trail around a 33-acre pond (a little rocky in places, so wear real shoes), and the 65-mile Mattabesett Trail crosses Durham's traprock ridges at Pisgah Mountain on its way through ten towns.

faq.question: How do I get to Durham?
faq.answer: By car — Route 17 runs north–south through town from I-91 in New Haven toward Middletown, with Route 68 crossing east–west and Routes 77, 79 and 147 running to Guilford, Madison and Middlefield. There is no rail station in Durham; the nearest CTrail Hartford Line stops are Meriden and Wallingford, and the nearest Shore Line East stops are Guilford and Madison.

faq.question: When is the Durham Fair?
faq.answer: The 2026 edition, the 106th annual, runs September 24–27 at the Durham Fairgrounds. It is Connecticut's largest agricultural fair and is run entirely by volunteers, held nearly every year since 1916 — interrupted only by 1938 hurricane damage, World War II and the 2020 pandemic.

faq.question: What is the Durham Book Company?
faq.answer: A lending library founded in 1733, one year after Benjamin Franklin organized his Philadelphia book club. Durham's library describes it as the second-oldest lending library in the country and the oldest in New England; it dissolved in the 1830s, but 39 of its volumes survive in the local history collection today.

faq.question: Is there a hotel in Durham?
faq.answer: No hotel, inn or B&B could be verified operating inside Durham. The nearest option is the Inn at Middletown, 70 Main Street, Middletown — a 100-room hotel in an 1800s-era building north of Durham via Route 17.

places.name: Durham Fairgrounds (Durham Fair)
places.summary: Home of the Durham Fair, founded in 1916 and run 100% by volunteers — Connecticut's largest agricultural fair. The 2026 edition, the 106th annual, runs September 24–27 with livestock and agricultural competitions, demolition derbies, tractor pulls, rides and live music. Admission: Thursday $10; Friday–Sunday $20 adults, $10 seniors 65+; free for children 11 and under, active military with ID and wheelchair users.

places.name: Millers Pond State Park
places.summary: A 33-acre pond ringed by an easy, flat trail — a little rocky in places, so wear real shoes — with rock outcrops used as natural fishing platforms for smallmouth bass and trout. No beach or boat launch; an alcohol ban is in place. Free parking, open 8 a.m. to sunset, leashed pets welcome.

places.name: Mattabesett Trail
places.address: Crosses Durham along the traprock ridges near Pisgah Mountain
places.summary: A 65-mile Blue-Blazed hiking trail along the southern Metacomet Ridge, passing through Guilford, Durham, Madison, Haddam, Middletown, North Branford, Wallingford, Middlefield, Meriden and Berlin; Pisgah Mountain is Durham's named landmark. Maintained by the Connecticut Forest & Park Association, part of an official state greenway; call CFPA at (860) 346-8733 for trailhead directions.

places.name: Durham Main Street Historic District
places.address: Roughly Maple Avenue and Main Street between Talcott Lane and Higganum Road, Durham, CT 06422
places.summary: Listed on the National Register on September 4, 1986, the district covers Durham's colonial-era village core along Main Street. The town's America 250 Committee runs periodic guided walking tours of the district — a leisurely 1.4-mile loop from the town green out to Route 68; contact the Community Center to check the current schedule.

places.name: Durham Public Library
places.summary: A direct descendant of the 1733 Durham Book Company, with 39 volumes from that original collection in its local history collection. Voted into being in 1894, it opened its first purpose-built home in 1902, expanded in 1985 and 1997, and completed an interior renovation in 2023. Open Monday–Thursday 9 a.m.–8 p.m., Friday–Saturday 10 a.m.–5 p.m.

places.name: Allyn Brook Park
places.summary: A Durham Recreation Department park with a rentable pavilion and a playground, next to the Durham Community Center. The playgrounds at both sites were renovated and rebuilt starting April 26, 2024. Pavilion rentals are handled through RecDesk; Recreation Department (860) 894-7836.

places.name: Hard Hat Tavern
places.summary: A tavern-restaurant on the Route 17 corridor and the only full restaurant liquor permit currently active in Durham, per Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection records. No website could be found — call ahead to confirm hours before visiting.

places.name: Deerfield Farm
places.summary: A small registered-Jersey dairy farm with an on-site store selling raw Jersey milk straight from the cow, flavored milks, yogurt and soft cheeses. Farm store open daily 10 a.m.–5:30 p.m.; text (860) 301-7828 to confirm before visiting.

links.note: CT Route 147 runs from Durham's town center directly north into Middlefield.
CT Route 79 runs from Durham's town center directly south to Madison.
CT Route 77, a scenic road along its whole length, connects Durham to Guilford.
